extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists, news executives, and public-policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Coding scheme and evaluative metrics for analyzing news content (soft vs. hard news) and audience responses; includes a detailed codebook for content analysis and measures of public perceptions and news effects. Intended for systematic content analysis across newspapers, magazines, and broadcast news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft news vs. hard news (definition/measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news: coverage of breaking events involving top leaders, major issues, or significant disruptions in daily life (e.g., earthquake, airline disaster) and stories with a public policy component. Soft news: stories that have no clear connection to policy issues; often more sensational, personality-centered, less time-bound, more practical, and incident-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft news can be defined as the complement of hard news or by characteristics (sensationalism, human-interest, incident emphasis, practical 'news you can use', vocabulary changes). The codebook uses a policy/component test and other indicators to classify stories. Use context: a crime story with no public-policy reference may be non-policy (soft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the story's form: (1) basically straight news/hard news (happened in past 24 hours; event/incident-based); (2) balanced mix of straight news and news analysis; (3) mainly news analysis (synthesizes material across times; includes motives/expectations); (4) feature/human interest; (5) verbatim text/interview, speech, or document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the lead of the story when coding type. Determine whether the piece is event-driven, interpretive, or feature oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of story
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the key focus: (1) current/ongoing event or development; (2) current incident (small, isolated personal event that doesn't have broader social implications); (3) update on past event; (4) update on past incident; (5) upcoming event; (6) non-event/non-incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'peg' may be current but code the story's focus (peg vs. focus distinction). Incidents are typically unexpected and personal (e.g., crime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salience of story (why this story is in today's news?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of newsworthiness/timeliness: (1) event/incident/anniversary of such magnitude/timeliness that no responsible editor could ignore it today; (2) event/incident of such magnitude that it had to be covered but not necessarily today; (3) event/incident of timeliness but small magnitude such that an editor could choose to cover or ignore it; (4) event/incident of smaller magnitude that an editor could choose to cover or ignore; (5) arbitrary placement (no event/peg making it newsworthy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code why the story appears today—magnitude and timeliness drive salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Origin of the piece: (1) news outlet byline story; (2) news outlet no byline; (3) news outlet’s wire service (e.g., chain); (4) compiled from wire services; (5) AP; (6) Reuters/UPI; (7) NYT or other news outlet-based wire service; (8) other identified source; (9) source not identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps assess whether story was generated internally or externally; check bylines and wire attributions carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story location/placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement in the publication or order in a newscast (front/local newspaper sections, top-of-newscast positions, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For television, placement is based on presentation order (note: some feeds may load backwards, count appropriately). Placement indicates prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story length
rubrics_metrics.description: Length in words (four-digit coding); overflow codes for indeterminate or >9998 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a quantitative measure of depth; very long pieces may be more interpretive/in-depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: News section (section/medium)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the section or medium: national, metro, other, indeterminate; or television news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits analysis to relevant sections (the Patterson study excluded sports/travel and 'conventional news broadcasts' excludes certain programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs. private frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story is framed in the public affairs/public realm (includes public actors e.g., government officials) or the private realm involving a salient actor (celebrity, private corporation, family matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public affairs stories may still lack policy content; a crime story may be coded public if it includes public actors like police statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy vs. non-policy frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story have relevance for public policy? (1) substantially policy related/policy relevant; (2) somewhat policy related; (3) non-policy related or inconsequential policy relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all public-affairs stories are policy related. Policy relatedness must be stated—e.g., a crime story that discusses public safety policy counts as policy relevant; a campaign scorekeeping story with no policy implications may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action vs. non-action frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story imply or state a need for action? (1) urgent need for action/problem requiring fix; (2) non-urgent need for action; (3) describes action already taken or being taken to resolve the problem; (4) no action component of note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If coded 1-3, follow with attribution of responsibility coding (who should act?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of responsibility frame
rubrics_metrics.description: When an action frame is present, who is identified as responsible or who should take action: (0) not applicable; (1) government/ public official; (2) group/collective/community or private institution; (3) private individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used only if previous action/non-action code indicates action relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: News you can use (utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story's primary/secondary purpose is to offer personal advice or practical guidance on health, money, safety, etc. (1) primary purpose; (2) secondary purpose; (3) not the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures 'news you can use' soft-news subcategory (practical consumer/health tips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual frame (episodic vs thematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the story mainly episodic (focused on a particular event/case-study) or thematic (places issue in broader social/trend context)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodic coverage tends toward incident-driven/soft framing; thematic coverage provides systemic/interpretive context and is closer to public affairs reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict vs non-conflict frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of conflict presented in the story: (1) substantial conflict; (2) some conflict; (3) no or inconsequential conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presentation style, not merely topic. If coded 1 or 2, also code nature of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of conflict (actual vs synthetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: If conflict present: (1) actual conflict (real, observable between participants); (2) synthetic conflict (conflict chiefly constructed by reporter via juxtaposition/speculation); (3) cannot determine; (0) not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes real disputes from reporter-instigated or artificial controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the story uses human examples/puts a human face on an issue or goes into private/personal life: (1) high human interest; (2) moderate; (3) slight; (4) none/incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest content is a key soft-news characteristic: look for personal vignettes, family references, emotional adjectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative vs positive frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall valence of the story: (1) clearly negative/unfavorable; (2) more negative than positive; (3) balanced mix; (4) more positive than negative; (5) clearly positive/favorable; (6) neutral/no clear valence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the story would be unfavorable if evaluated by a press secretary; used to measure critical/negative tone across coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of 'breathlessness' or hype in presentation: (1) high sensationalism; (2) moderate sensationalism; (3) low sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge tone, adjectives, framing. Sensationalism is a soft-news characteristic and should be assessed in context of reporter presentation, not just subject matter magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story ambiance (tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone regardless of topic: (1) serious/important; (2) matter-of-fact; (3) lighthearted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiance interacts with other frames (e.g., a lighthearted piece can still be policy relevant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic style
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the piece is descriptive (tells 'what' happened straightforwardly) or interpretive/analytical/evaluative (analyzes, explains, or evaluates while describing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive style aligns with explanatory journalism; descriptive style aligns with straightforward event reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft news / hard news coding (aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall classification scale: (1) definitely soft news story; (2) mostly soft; (3) mixed about even; (4) mostly hard news; (5) definitely hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a summary measure informed by the other frames (policy content, human interest, sensationalism, contextual frame, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic arena
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic scope: foreign/international with no significant U.S. component; foreign/international with significant U.S. component; national with significant foreign link; national; regional (multi-state); state; local; none/no location context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to analyze distribution of soft/hard coverage across geographic scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story lead (type of lead subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who/what leads the story: political/governmental personality; nonpolitical personality (artist, celebrity, criminal); expert person (professor, economist, doctor); ordinary/unknown person; institution or government agency; group/organization; corporation/business entity; country/state/city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads that center personalities (especially nonpolitical celebrities) are indicative of soft news; expert-led leads often imply interpretive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main actor / realm code
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify principal actor/realm when applicable: e.g., President/White House; Cabinet officer/federal agency; Member of Congress; Supreme Court/federal judiciary; etc., or not applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for tracking which institutional actors receive what tone/quantity of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major topic code
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical categorization of the story: government & policy, politics (campaign/vote/strategy), political scandal, political personality, business & commerce, celebrity, celebrity crime/scandal, crime, natural disasters, manmade disasters, science, technology, medicine, personal health, media, entertainment/arts/fashion/travel, food, religion, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to analyze topical composition of news and shifts toward soft subjects (celebrity, entertainment) vs public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major issue code
rubrics_metrics.description: If policy/government topic, code the specific issue area: economy, unemployment/jobs, international trade, environment, taxes, government spending, inflation, health, welfare/poverty, education, housing, public safety, war & peace, terrorism, national defense, foreign affairs, immigration, race issues, women's issues, abortion, criminal justice, drugs, police conduct, science, technology policy, media performance, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granular issue coding allows measurement of public-policy content proportion and trends over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major context frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall framing orientation of the story: (1) ambition and power frame (winning/losing, tactical maneuvering); (2) conflict frame (blame, infighting); (3) cooperation frame (working together, collective effort); (4) problem/policy frame (identifying/explaining problems and attempts to resolve them); (5) human interest frame; (6) none of these frames (describe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame choice affects whether a story contributes to public understanding (problem/policy) or to personalization/infotainment (ambition/power, human interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: DICTION / vocabulary measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual vocabulary categories measured by DICTION: COLLECTIVES (words reflecting categorical social groupings), SELF-REFERENCE (first-person references), HUMAN INTEREST (personal pronouns, family terms, generic friend/baby), COMPLEXITY (average word length), and other DICTION categories (35 total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in frequency of these word categories indicate shifts toward softer (more SELF-REFERENCE, HUMAN INTEREST, lower COMPLEXITY) or harder (more COLLECTIVES) reporting vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of stories without public policy component
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the percentage of stories that have no clear public-policy connection (used to quantify soft news proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patterson study reports an increase from <35% in 1980 to roughly 50% by the 1990s across outlets; use policy frame codes to compute this metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism prevalence metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of stories coded with moderate to high sensationalism (indicator of softening news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the early 1980s ~25% moderate-high sensationalism vs nearly 40% later. Use SENSATIONALISM FRAME coding to compute trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest prevalence metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of stories with a human-interest element (high/moderate/slight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to detect rise in personalized stories; Patterson reports human-interest stories grew from <11% to ~26%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime/disaster incidence metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of stories whose subject is crime or disaster (dramatic incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rising incidence indicates incident-driven softening; examine MAJOR TOPIC and HUMAN-INTEREST coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative coverage metric (tone toward public actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of negative vs positive coverage for public actors (e.g., negative coverage of presidential candidates, Congress, agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NEGATIVE/POSITIVE FRAME across stories about specific actors to track critical journalism trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience perception bipolar measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Public survey items asking whether the news is: informative/uninformative, interesting/boring, enjoyable/not enjoyable, depressing/uplifting, negative/positive, sensational/serious, superficial/thorough, biased/fair, misleading/accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bipolar items are used to capture public attitudes toward news quality and tone; responses predict reported attention changes and preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience preference for hard vs soft news (direct and headline tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey measures: direct question whether respondents prefer news about major events/issues (hard) vs specific incidents like crime or fire (soft); Headline Test: interest rating for representative hard and soft news headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine direct preference and headline interest to validate preferences and detect response bias; Patterson finds majority preference for hard news and headline test confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular news consumption metrics by medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of respondents who regularly (nearly every day) read newspaper news pages, watch local TV news, watch national/broadcast/cable news, or listen to radio news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare hard vs soft news consumers: hard-news-preferring respondents consume more news across most media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived reasons for reduced news attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey items asking non-regular consumers why they reduced attention (e.g., 'politics has become disgusting', 'too much crime', 'too many fluff stories', 'too negative', 'seldom presents positive things').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These open/structured reasons provide evidence for soft news and critical journalism effects on audience decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline-level interest probability (probability a random reader/viewer finds a soft story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability lines (as in Figure 7) representing the probability that a randomly exposed reader/viewer would find a soft news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to model how likely soft vs hard stories attract undifferentiated audiences; derived from headline test and content distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings / audience change vs quality correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative metric linking measured quality of newscasts (e.g., Project for Excellence rankings) to changes in audience ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to test whether higher-quality (hard-news-oriented) newscasts have better audience performance over time; evidence suggests many high-quality stations saw ratings increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical journalism indicators (tone and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators of critical journalism: rising negative coverage of politicians and institutions, investigation-oriented reporting, less deference to private lives of officials, and increasing skepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure via NEGATIVE/POSITIVE FRAME, nature of coverage (investigative/analytical), and trends in negative-valence proportions over time; relate to public trust metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public trust and political interest metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey trends in trust in government, belief in politicians' honesty, and self-reported interest in public affairs (e.g., 'most of the time' vs 'now and then').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical survey series (e.g., NES) to relate changes in media tone/coverage to broader civic attitudes; Patterson links declines to negative/critical coverage among other factors.
